summary: Specifies the EAP key hierarchy and a framework for transporting and using key material generated by EAP methods. It includes a system-level security analysis and checks conditions for meeting the guidelines in RFC 4962. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5247 explains how keys created during EAP authentication are named, transported and used by network access systems. It separates authentication from the later exchange that creates keys for protecting network traffic, and sets rules to limit where key material can go.

subtitle: How EAP keys are named, delivered to network layers and managed securely.

tldr.problem: EAP methods can derive keys, but EAP does not by itself define how lower layers receive and use those keys, identify them, manage their lifetimes or create security associations.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5247 defines the EAP key hierarchy, exported key names and parameters, a typical three-phase exchange, and requirements for lower-layer handshakes and key handling. It also analyzes the framework against the system-level requirements in RFC 4962.
tldr.outcome: The framework separates authentication methods from lower-layer key use and requires strict limits on key scope and sharing. RFC 5247 updates RFC 3748 and is updated by RFC 8940.

facts.label: Default key lifetime
facts.value: 8 hours (recommended when no lifetime is known)

today: RFC 5247 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3748. It has been updated by RFC 8940, so read it together with that update.

sections.title: What the Key Framework Covers
sections.content:
The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) lets a peer and an EAP server authenticate using a selected method. A method can generate keying material and export keys and parameters such as identities and a conversation identifier.

RFC 5247 defines the hierarchy and gives a framework for moving and using the exported material. EAP itself does not manage the lower-layer security associations that protect later network traffic, and it does not specify how every lower layer transports or uses keys.

The RFC analyzes the system-level conditions needed to meet the key-management guidance in RFC 4962. It covers EAP methods, authentication, authorization and accounting (AAA) transport, lower layers and post-EAP security association protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: An EAP method can create secret keys while a device proves its identity to a network. This RFC sets rules for how the network carries and uses those keys after authentication.

sections.title: The Three Phases
sections.content:
The typical process has three phases. Phase 0 is discovery, when the peer locates an authenticator and learns its capabilities. Phase 1 is authentication: phase 1a runs EAP and derives key material, while optional phase 1b transports key material from a backend server to the authenticator using AAA.

Phase 2 is the Secure Association Protocol between the peer and authenticator. It establishes a unicast association and may establish a multicast association. Discovery and phase 2 are handled by the lower layer; phase 1b is typically handled by a AAA protocol such as RADIUS or Diameter.

Successful EAP authentication does not by itself mean the peer has joined the network. The peer's commitment to use the network is established through the security association in phase 2.
sections.plainLanguage: The process first finds an authenticator, then authenticates the peer, then sets up keys for network traffic. Authentication alone does not establish the later protected connection.

sections.title: The EAP Key Hierarchy
sections.content:
The hierarchy begins with the long-term credential used by the EAP method, such as a pre-shared key or a private key. The method derives local keys, including Transient EAP Keys (TEKs), and exported material: the Master Session Key (MSK), Extended Master Session Key (EMSK), and an optional Initialization Vector (IV).

A method that supports key derivation must export an MSK and an EMSK of at least 64 octets each. The IV is deprecated and optional. The EMSK must remain within the EAP peer and EAP server; it must not be shared with another entity or be derivable from material shared outside those parties.

Methods that support key derivation and mutual authentication should export a Session-Id and peer identity; they may also export server identities. New EAP method specifications must define Peer-Id, Server-Id and Session-Id. The MSK and EMSK names combine the Session-Id with an indication of which key is meant.
sections.plainLanguage: EAP methods create some keys for their own use and export other keys for the network. The exported keys have names, and the EMSK must stay with the peer and EAP server.

sections.title: Four EAP Invariants
sections.content:
The framework requires EAP methods to preserve four properties. Mode independence means a method behaves the same whether the authenticator runs it locally or passes EAP messages to a backend server. Media independence means methods do not depend on the network layer carrying EAP; channel-binding data is treated as opaque by the method.

Method independence means a pass-through authenticator does not need code for every method it forwards. Ciphersuite independence means EAP exports material that can be used with lower-layer ciphersuites negotiated outside EAP.

Algorithms that derive Transient Session Keys (TSKs) must not depend on the EAP method, though TEK derivation may be method-specific. Keeping these responsibilities separate avoids requiring an EAP method to change whenever a lower layer adds a ciphersuite.
sections.plainLanguage: EAP methods should work across different network media, authenticator designs and authentication methods. The lower layer chooses how to protect traffic, so EAP keys must not depend on that choice.

sections.title: How Lower Layers Handle Keys
sections.content:
After EAP authentication, exported material and parameters pass to the lower layer and, when present, the AAA layer. A lower layer must not export EAP keys or use them for another lower layer. Key material delivered to one entity must not be transported onward to another entity, except that server-side material may be replicated to the authenticator's AAA layer; the EMSK is excluded.

The EAP, peer and authenticator layers must not modify or cache material as it passes between the EAP method and lower layer. A lower layer may cache keys only when it explicitly supports caching, and a new lower-layer specification must describe that behavior.

A AAA layer that has transported keys must delete them and must not retain them. The RFC also recommends identifying peers and authenticators explicitly, rather than relying on port or endpoint addresses, because either device may have multiple ports or virtual identities.
sections.plainLanguage: A key delivered to one network layer must stay within that layer and its authorized devices. A AAA system must delete transported keys after sending them.

sections.title: Secure Association and Key Lifetimes
sections.content:
EAP derives keys but does not negotiate lower-layer security associations, coordinate key installation or deletion, negotiate exported-key lifetimes, or guarantee fresh TSKs when keys are cached. A post-EAP Secure Association Protocol is intended to handle these tasks between the peer and authenticator.

The protocol should name the parties, confirm that both possess the key material, negotiate capabilities securely, identify keys and associations, and synchronize activation and deletion. When the lower layer caches keys, a Secure Association Protocol is required and must derive fresh unicast and multicast TSKs even if the transported key material is reused. Nonces or counters can contribute to fresh derived keys.

A derived key must not outlive its parent key. If no lifetime can be learned, the RFC recommends a default lifetime of 8 hours. It also notes known problems with the RADIUS key-wrap mechanism and points to running RADIUS over IPsec as the recommended approach.
sections.plainLanguage: A second exchange between the peer and authenticator sets up the keys used for traffic and keeps both sides synchronized. Even if an older key is reused, the exchange must create fresh traffic keys when caching is supported.

sections.title: Risks When Handoffs Skip AAA
sections.content:
Handoff methods can reduce delay by pre-authenticating at a future authenticator, distributing keys in advance or reusing cached keys. These methods can skip or shorten phases of the normal exchange, but bypassing the backend AAA step also bypasses its delivery of keys and authorizations.

A handoff is correct only if the new authenticator applies the same authorizations that a full AAA exchange would have produced. Otherwise a peer might gain a service it is not allowed to use, network-wide state such as concurrent-session counts may be lost, or the peer may gain elevated privileges.

The RFC says a handoff should fail if it would result in incorrect authorization. For example, a new authenticator may support different VLANs or security services from the previous one, so copied authorization information may not be valid there.
sections.plainLanguage: Skipping the backend authorization check can make a handoff faster, but the new authenticator might grant the wrong access. The handoff should fail if it cannot preserve the authorization a full check would provide.

sections.title: System-Level Security Requirements
sections.content:
The threat model assumes an attacker can observe, alter, forge, replay or reroute messages and may compromise a peer or authenticator. The analysis checks key management against requirements including independent protection of devices, algorithm negotiation, authentication of parties, confidentiality, replay protection, fresh keys, limited key scope and authorization.

For example, a compromised pass-through authenticator can give the peer misleading information about the network. Channel binding lets the peer and server compare protected lower-layer parameters. Proof that two parties possess the same key does not, by itself, prove that both were authorized to hold it.

The RFC notes that RADIUS without IPsec cannot negotiate its integrity algorithm and relies on MD5. It also warns that cached key state can create denial-of-service risks and that AAA systems must limit which entities receive keying material.
sections.plainLanguage: The security analysis considers attackers who can interfere with authentication messages or compromise network devices. It emphasizes checking device identities, limiting where keys can go and confirming that parties are authorized, not merely that they share a key.

items.title: Mode
items.text: Methods work whether the authenticator is local or passes EAP through.

items.title: Media
items.text: Methods do not depend on the lower layer that carries EAP.

items.title: Method
items.text: A pass-through authenticator need not implement the methods it forwards.

items.title: Ciphersuite
items.text: EAP keys work with the ciphersuite negotiated by the lower layer.
